newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate approves international rubber treaty.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate approves international rubber treaty.

text.p: The Senate Wednesday approved a four-year International Natural Rubber Agreement designed to control the price and supply of the commodity, which is essential to a host of major American industries.
The Senate approved the agreement by voice vote. The House does not debate treaties.

The United States has entered into two previous rubber pacts, in 1979 and 1987. But the Clinton administration has said this is the last such treaty the United States intends to agree to, saying it is time to move toward a free market.

Supporters of the agreement said it was needed to prevent wide price swings and protect domestic industries. The United States is the world's largest user of natural rubber, but produces none of its own.

"Virtually all Americans, whether they're aware of it or not, depend on rubber products every day of the week. Any American who drives a car or rides a bus or takes a taxi to work relies on rubber products," said Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms.
"Many Americans may not be aware that we are completely dependent on foreign countries for our supply of natural rubber," the North Carolian Republican said.
Opponents charged that the International Natural Rubber Organisation, established under the agreements, was basically a cartel that artificially set prices and hurt American consumers.

"Big labour, big business, importers all favour the treaty. People who are concerned about the taxpayers of this country and consumers of this country will want to vote against this treaty," said Colorado Republican Sen. Hank Brown.
In a letter to Congress earlier this summer, President Clinton said U.S. participation in one final pact was needed to give business and labour time to prepare for a free market in rubber.
He also said the agreement would strengthen U.S. relations with Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, which together account for about 80 percent of the world production of natural rubber.

The agreement stabilises prices through use of a buffer stock of not more than 550,000 tons. The buffer stock is used to keep rubber prices, which in the past have fluctuated wildly, within a set price band.
Both producing and consuming national contribute funds to the buffer stock, according to their share of world rubber exports and imports.
The pact contains language barring members of the rubber organisation from acting to manipulate rubber prices or restrict supplies outside the agreement.
